summary: Kole Jain grades SaaS landing pages on four levels, from a template-like level one ("you'd be lucky to get $500" for it, 2 out of 10) to a crafted level four (well over $10,000, 10 out of 10), and walks each level through the same dimensions: layout, visuals, typography, copy, navigation, color, animation and page flow. The path runs from stock images and alternating text-and-image rows, through a stacked hero with the real product dashboard, to zoomed-in and then purpose-crafted product visuals, bento grids, clickable multi-selects, mega menus and copy that says how the product helps rather than what it does. He argues the jump from good to great is many small details, such as a blur effect on the click-through multi-select, a mega menu that slides content instead of closing and reopening, and a call to action that appears on hover only when needed. For a design system, it gives a ready audit checklist for marketing pages, a set of layout and navigation patterns with a clear order of maturity, and rules about where accent color should come from.
key_ideas: A landing page can work functionally and still look like a template, because nobody made any design decisions.
Alternating text-left, image-right rows all the way down reads as a template unless the page adds variety.
Show the actual product instead of stock images; later, zoom in on its important parts, and finally craft visuals to show exactly what the product does.
Letting color pops come from the product visuals is more vibrant and professional than spreading an accent color over everything that will take it.
Navigation needs hierarchy: the sign-up action and the more important links should stand out, and the menu should be balanced rather than weighted to one side.
Two buttons with the same label imply they go to the same place, which builds the right mental model.
Copy should get shorter and punchier, and at the top level move from describing what the product does to how it helps.
Swapping a row of cards for a bento grid, and a static card row for a clickable multi-select, adds room, interactivity and variety.
At level three designers become product designers, adding brand elements such as a badge, a set of logos and a link to a social proof page.
Good page flow means each section leads into the next instead of sections dropped one on top of another.
Motion matures from none, to simple load animations, to smooth hover effects and fluid sliders, to small high-quality touches like a blur effect.
The difference between good and great is almost never one big thing; it is attention to detail.
A level four page needs no custom illustrations or 3D, only well-crafted UI with strong attention to detail.

topics.name: Landing pages
topics.summary: Four levels of SaaS landing page UI, each judged on layout, visuals, typography, copy, navigation, color, animation and page flow, with what to fix to reach the next level.

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Level one has flat hierarchy in type and navigation; level three builds clear hierarchy through color and size, slightly overdone so the headline dominates the sub-line.

topics.name: Navigation and sidebars
topics.summary: Moves from a flat, right-weighted menu, to outlined key buttons with centered links and small hover dropdowns (though the menu is still slightly too large), to a mega menu, to a mega menu that stays open and slides content left or right.

topics.name: Content and microcopy
topics.summary: Cut vague, long copy and the redundant company name; make headlines shorter and punchier; at level four, describe how the product helps instead of what it does.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: Level one applies blue haphazardly and leans on images for color; level two takes color pops from the product dashboard with white buttons; level four threads color through curated visuals.

topics.name: Typography
topics.summary: One font throughout is good; tighten things up and build a stronger hierarchy, then at level four loosen spacing slightly and use text widths to form leading lines into the content.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Moves from an alternating side-by-side layout to a stacked hero, then vertical lines framing the content, then a more flexible layout molded around the content.

topics.name: Cards and sections
topics.summary: Replaces a row of four cards with a bento grid and a three-card row with a clickable multi-select, producing shorter, more compact sections.

topics.name: Icons and imagery
topics.summary: Stock images unrelated to the product throw the page off; the product dashboard, zoomed and later purpose-crafted, should carry the visuals, with images only where they make sense.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Level three adds subtle hover effects on the dashboard and bento; level four adds a blur effect to the multi-select and a call to action that appears on hover over the logo section.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: Animation grows from none, to simple load animations, to smooth transitions, to high-quality details; key interactions usually develop later than the other principles.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: The top-nav and hero call to action should share a label when they go to the same place; level two swaps to white buttons, and level three weaves the blue back in while keeping the primary call to action, with an icon.

topics.name: Shape and corner radius
topics.summary: Sharp-edged images next to rounded buttons create a disconnect on the level one page.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: The gap between okay and converting pages is knowing what level you are at and what to fix next; great comes from many small details rather than one big change.

topics.name: Freelancing and pricing work
topics.summary: Attaches rough prices to each level: you'd be lucky to get $500, about $2,000, about six to ten thousand dollars, and well over $10,000.

quotes: Most SaaS landing pages look okay, but okay doesn't get you customers.
the difference between good and great is almost never one big thing
transform from what it does to how it helps

rules.rule: Do not alternate text-left, image-right rows all the way down a landing page; vary the section layouts.
rules.why: The alternating layout makes the page look like a template; professional sites that use it add good variety throughout.
rules.evidence: text on the left, image on the right, alternating basically all the way down

rules.rule: Use a stacked hero layout instead of a side-by-side hero.
rules.why: It steps the page away from being a template and lets it breathe a little more.
rules.evidence: much more modern stacked approach

rules.rule: Show the actual product (for example its dashboard) instead of stock images that have little to do with the product.
rules.why: Unrelated stock images throw the whole page off; the product dashboard is a massive improvement.
rules.evidence: literal stock image

rules.rule: Zoom in on the important parts of the product dashboard to curate exactly what the viewer sees, and at the highest level craft the visual to show exactly what the product does.
rules.why: A full dashboard that is not perfectly framed does not draw attention to anything in particular; zooming in curates exactly what the viewer sees.
rules.evidence: zoom in on the actual important parts of the dashboard

rules.rule: Do not pair sharp-edged images with rounded-corner buttons on the same page.
rules.why: The source calls it a disconnect that, with the level one page's other problems, means the page does not encourage you to keep scrolling.
rules.evidence: disconnect between the sharp edges of the images and the rounded corners

rules.rule: Use one font throughout the landing page.
rules.why: The source calls using the same font throughout good even on the level one page.
rules.evidence: we're using the same font throughout, which is good

rules.rule: Build a clear typographic hierarchy through color and size.
rules.why: Level one's weak hierarchy is one of its problems; level three makes a massive step forward with it.
rules.evidence: clear hierarchy forming through the use of color and size

rules.rule: Do not let the headline dominate so much that the sub-line loses out.
rules.why: The level three hierarchy is slightly overdone, so the headline dominates at the expense of the sub-line.
rules.evidence: headline dominates at the expense of the sub-line

rules.rule: Use slightly looser type spacing and work with text widths so the lines lead into the content.
rules.why: This is how level four balances its typography.
rules.evidence: slightly looser spacing and work with the widths

rules.rule: Keep hero copy short and punchy; cut vague, long blocks of text.
rules.why: No one stops to read a long block of text, especially once the visuals carry more of the narrative.
rules.evidence: No one is stopping to read a block of text like this

rules.rule: Do not repeat the company name in the copy when it is already visible on screen.
rules.why: The source says there is no need to mention it when it is already right there.
rules.evidence: we don't need to mention the company name when it's right here

rules.rule: Write feature copy about how the product helps the user, not only what it does.
rules.why: Moving from what the product does to how it inherently helps is much more valuable; it is the copy step from level three to level four.
rules.evidence: transform from what it does to how it helps

rules.rule: Give the navigation menu hierarchy: make the sign-up action and the more important links (such as Product) stand out, for example with an outline on the most important buttons.
rules.why: A flat menu where every item looks identical does not draw the eye to the most important action.
rules.evidence: Every item looks virtually identical

rules.rule: Balance the navigation bar, for example by centering the secondary links, instead of weighting everything to the right.
rules.why: A menu heavily weighted to the right does not balance the website well.
rules.evidence: the other links are centered to balance that menu out

rules.rule: Give the hero call to action the same label as the top navigation call to action when both go to the same place.
rules.why: Matching labels strongly imply the two buttons go to the same place, which is the correct mental model.
rules.evidence: now these two have the same label

rules.rule: Add small dropdowns on hover to the larger, more important navigation links.
rules.why: Level two adds them as part of giving the menu hierarchy; later levels expand them into a mega menu.
rules.evidence: small drop-downs on hover of the larger, more important links

rules.rule: Do not apply the accent color haphazardly to everything that will reasonably take it.
rules.why: On level one, blue applied haphazardly makes the buttons dominate the text.
rules.evidence: applied pretty haphazardly to anything that will reasonably take it

rules.rule: Do not rely largely on images to supply the page's color.
rules.why: Level one pages lean on images for color because color is hard to nail, and it overwhelmingly misses the mark.
rules.evidence: rely largely on images to do a lot of that heavy lifting

rules.rule: Let the color pops come from the product visuals, which allows neutral (white) buttons.
rules.why: The source calls it a much more vibrant and professional way to add color, and it makes the swap to white buttons possible.
rules.evidence: The color pops now come from the dashboard

rules.rule: Thread color through the whole page using curated visuals, with images only where they make sense.
rules.why: Zooming into the product can strip color out; curating the visuals lets color return across the page.
rules.evidence: thread the color throughout the landing page expertly

rules.rule: Frame the page content with vertical lines that run the length of the page.
rules.why: It structures the page and easily keeps it responsive on much larger screens.
rules.evidence: frames in the content with vertical lines

rules.rule: Replace a plain row of four cards with a bento grid.
rules.why: A bento grid gives the content a little more room to expand and breathe.
rules.evidence: four cards to a Bento grid

rules.rule: Replace a static three-card row with a multi-select the visitor can click through.
rules.why: It adds interactivity and variety and leads to shorter, more compact sections.
rules.evidence: three-card row to a multi-select

rules.rule: Add brand-strengthening elements such as a badge, a set of logos and a button that takes visitors to a social proof page.
rules.why: This is where designers stop being UI designers and become product designers.
rules.evidence: adding in elements to strengthen the brand

rules.rule: Use a mega menu for the most important navigation links.
rules.why: It makes navigating easy and signals depth, that the product is worth exploring.
rules.evidence: beautiful mega menu for the most important links

rules.rule: When moving between mega menu items, keep the menu open and slide the content left or right instead of fully closing and reopening it.
rules.why: Side by side, keeping it open is much smoother than a full close to a full open.
rules.evidence: we keep it open and bump the content out to the left or right

rules.rule: Instead of a permanent button under the logo section, show a call to action on hover only when it is needed.
rules.why: The call to action appears only when it is needed; it is one of the level four details.
rules.evidence: a call to action that appears only when it's needed

rules.rule: Polish the click-through multi-select with a blur effect (the transcript does not say exactly where the blur is applied or how strong it is).
rules.why: The source says this simple, high-quality change takes the component from 8 out of 10 to 10 out of 10.
rules.evidence: With that blur effect

rules.rule: Add subtle hover effects and interaction to the product visuals and bento tiles, and make sliders transition fluidly.
rules.why: The source counts these subtle animations among the smaller details that make level three an 8 out of 10.
rules.evidence: The dashboard now has some subtle hover effects

rules.rule: Add simple load animations rather than leaving the page static with only a basic hover effect.
rules.why: Level one's lone hover effect does not make the site come to life; level two's load animations add much-needed movement.
rules.evidence: simple load animations

rules.rule: Design each section to lead into the next, for example fading out the dashboard to segue into the features, instead of stacking unrelated sections.
rules.why: Level one feels like sections dropped one on top of the other; good flow encourages visitors to keep scrolling.
rules.evidence: the fade out of the dashboard segues nicely

decisions.question: How should the hero section be laid out?

options.name: Side by side (text left, image right)
options.effect: Looks like a template, especially when the alternation repeats down the page.
options.when: Only with good variety elsewhere on the page, as some professional sites do.

options.name: Stacked
options.effect: More modern, and lets the page breathe a little more.
options.when: The level two step away from a template.

decisions.recommendation: Stacked; the source says it steps the page away from being a template.

decisions.question: What should the main landing page visuals show?

options.name: Stock images
options.effect: Little to do with the product; throws the whole page off.

options.name: The full product dashboard
options.effect: A massive improvement and a source of color, but not perfectly framed and draws attention to nothing in particular.

options.name: Zoomed-in crops of the dashboard
options.effect: Curates exactly what the viewer sees, but can remove charts and reduce color.

options.name: Visuals crafted for the page
options.effect: Shows exactly what the product does and lets color thread through the page; feels made for the website.

decisions.recommendation: Crafted product visuals; the source says level four crafts the visuals to show exactly what the product does.
decisions.evidence: We're crafting to be exactly what we need

decisions.question: Where should the page's color come from?

options.name: Accent applied to anything, images carry the rest
options.effect: The blue dominates the text and the images overwhelmingly miss the mark.

options.name: Color pops from the product visuals, with white buttons
options.effect: More vibrant and professional.

options.name: Accent woven into the primary call to action, with color threaded through curated visuals
options.effect: Color returns across the page while the accent still marks the primary action.

decisions.recommendation: Take color from curated product visuals and keep the accent for the primary call to action; the source calls the scattered accent haphazard.
decisions.evidence: The color pops now come from the dashboard

decisions.question: How should the top navigation be designed?

options.name: Flat menu
options.effect: Every item looks identical, nothing draws the eye to sign-up, and it is weighted heavily to the right.

options.name: Outlined key buttons, centered links and small hover dropdowns
options.effect: Hierarchy and balance appear; the most important links open small dropdowns on hover.

options.name: Mega menu for the most important links
options.effect: Easy navigation that signals depth and a product worth exploring.

decisions.question: How should a mega menu animate when moving between items?

options.name: Full close to full open
options.effect: Works, but less smooth.

options.name: Stay open and slide the content left or right
options.effect: Same structure, much smoother side by side.

decisions.recommendation: Stay open and slide the content; the source says it is so much smoother.
decisions.evidence: we keep it open and bump the content out to the left or right

options.name: A row of four cards
options.effect: Less interesting.

options.name: A bento grid
options.effect: Gives content more room to expand and breathe; more compact, modern sections.

decisions.evidence: four cards to a Bento grid

decisions.question: How should a set of three feature highlights be shown?

options.name: A static three-card row
options.effect: Plain and static.

options.name: A clickable multi-select
options.effect: Adds interactivity and variety and shortens the section.

options.name: A multi-select with a blur effect
options.effect: The same component with a simple, high-quality blur that the source rates 10 out of 10.

decisions.recommendation: A clickable multi-select, polished with a blur transition at the top level.

decisions.question: What should the landing page copy focus on?

options.name: Long, vague text
options.effect: Nobody stops to read it.

options.name: Shorter, punchier headline and related subtext
options.effect: A substantial improvement, though it can still be too long.

process.detail: Grade the landing page on each dimension the video uses: layout, visuals, typography, copy, navigation, color, animation and page flow, and note which level each one is at.

Switch to a stacked hero, replace stock images with the real product dashboard, take color from the dashboard and use white buttons, tighten type, shorten the headline, give the menu hierarchy and balance, match the two call-to-action labels, and add simple load animations.

Zoom in on the important parts of the dashboard, frame the content with vertical lines, turn the four-card row into a bento grid and the three-card row into a multi-select, add brand elements (badge, logos, social proof link), add a mega menu, weave the accent back into the primary call to action with an icon, and smooth out hover effects and sliders.

Craft the visuals to show exactly what the product does, loosen the layout and the type spacing, rewrite copy from what it does to how it helps, thread color through the page, and polish motion details: a blur on the multi-select, a mega menu that slides instead of reopening, and a hover call to action on the logo section.
Walk the page top to bottom and make each section lead into the next, for example fading out the dashboard into the features, so visitors keep scrolling.

caveats: Sponsor segment for Mobbin (curated library of real websites and apps, a 20% discount link, almost a thousand curated CTA sections); excluded from rules, and his claim that he uses it for research is part of the sponsor read.
The prices and scores for each level are the creator's rough estimates and opinions, not measured data.

No exact values are stated: no durations, curves, blur amounts, radii, sizes or colors. The designs are shown on screen and only described loosely in the transcript, and no media list was available. Where the level four blur is applied is only visible on screen.
The four example pages come from the creator's Figma files linked in the description; they appear to be his own mock-ups rather than live sites [inferred].
Ends with a plug for his other video breaking down seven layouts from the top 50 software companies.
Auto-caption errors: 'Mobb in' is Mobbin; 'Whereas as had many straight lines' and 'how How make yours' are garbled but do not change the meaning.
